questions.stem: When was MPC established?
questions.passage_context:
India's monetary policy framework has evolved significantly over the past decade. The 2016 establishment of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) — a 6-member body with 3 RBI representatives and 3 government nominees — marked a paradigm shift. Decisions now follow Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) with a 4±2% target band. Before MPC, rate decisions were made by the RBI Governor alone, often subject to political pressure.

The MPC's approach is data-driven. It analyses CPI inflation, food prices, fuel prices, demand-supply dynamics, and growth indicators before setting the repo rate. Communication has also improved — minutes are released two weeks after each meeting, and the Governor explains decisions in extensive press conferences. This transparency reduces market volatility around policy events.

Recent years have tested the framework. The COVID-19 pandemic forced the MPC to cut the repo rate to a historic low of 4% (May 2020) and inject liquidity through extraordinary measures. Subsequent inflation spikes — driven by oil prices, supply disruptions, and food costs — required gradual rate hikes. By 2024, the repo rate stood at 6.5%, and inflation had moderated to under 5%.

The next phase will face new challenges. Climate-related inflation (food shocks from extreme weather), geopolitical premiums (oil supply disruptions), and the implications of CBDC (e₹) all sit on MPC's agenda. Coordination with fiscal policy — particularly during stagflationary episodes — requires nuanced judgement.

What seemed institutional gymnastics in 2016 has become foundational architecture. The MPC framework's independence, transparency, and data-driven approach have served India well. Continued evolution — incorporating climate-related risks, refining the inflation index, and strengthening communication — will determine whether RBI maintains its credibility as one of the world's most respected central banks.
questions.explanation: **2016.** Para 1: 'The 2016 establishment of the Monetary Policy Committee.'
